entry: Sociological category of people who have less power than a dominant group in a society. In common usage the term means a group with the fewest members, or less than half of a population, but academics usually define it by relative disadvantage rather than numbers. In South Africa under [[Apartheid]], black Africans were called a minority group although they outnumbered white Europeans, who held nearly all social, economic and political power. Membership is typically based on observable characteristics such as [[Ethnicity]], [[Race (human categorization)|race]], religion, sexual orientation or disability, and a person may belong to several minority groups at once. Minority group members often face [[Discrimination]] in housing, employment, healthcare and education, through individual acts and structural inequalities. Supporters of minority rights seek laws that protect such groups and grant them equal legal status. Critics argue that this focus on power underplays factors within groups.

Creature of [[Greek mythology]] with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man. The Minotaur was kept at the center of the Labyrinth, a maze built by Daedalus and his son [[Icarus]] for King Minos of [[Crete]]. According to tradition, every nine years [[Athens]] had to send fourteen young citizens as sacrificial victims to the creature, as punishment for the death of Minos's son Androgeus. The Minotaur was slain by the Athenian hero Theseus, who found his way out with a golden thread given to him by Ariadne, the king's daughter. In the myth, the creature was born after the god [[Poseidon]], punishing Minos, arranged for his wife Pasiphaë to fall in love with a bull. Later, the notion of minotaurs as a race of beings became common in 20th-century fantasy fiction.

Capital and largest city of [[Belarus]]. Minsk has a special administrative status as the capital and lies on the Svislach River. With about two million inhabitants, it is the 11th-most populous city in Europe, and it is one of the administrative capitals of the [[Commonwealth of Independent States]] and the Eurasian Economic Union. First mentioned in 1067, it was annexed by the [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] in 1242 and received town privileges in 1499. It came under the [[Russian Empire]] in 1793 as a result of the Second Partition of Poland. From 1919 to 1991 it was the capital of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, and after the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] it became the capital of independent Belarus. Heavy damage under Nazi occupation during [[World War II]] was followed by postwar rebuilding.

Unit of time equal to 60 seconds, or one-sixtieth of an hour. The word comes from the Latin *pars minuta prima*, "first small part," and the [[Second|second]] takes its name from the "second small part." [[Al-Biruni]] first divided the hour sexagesimally into minutes, seconds, thirds and fourths in 1000 CE. In 1577 Jost Bürgi made the first clock with a minute hand, for astronomer Tycho Brahe. Minute hands became possible in watches only after Thomas Tompion's invention of the hairspring in 1675. The minute is accepted for use with the [[International System of Units|SI]], though the second is the SI base unit of time. In UTC, a minute occasionally has 61 seconds because of [[Leap second|leap seconds]].

First epoch of the [[Neogene]] Period, about 23 to 5 million years ago. Named by Scottish geologist [[Charles Lyell]] from [[Ancient Greek]] words meaning "less recent," because it has 18% fewer modern marine invertebrates than the [[Pliocene]]. In the early Miocene, Afro-Arabia's collision with [[Eurasia]] enabled the dispersal of [[Proboscidea|proboscideans]] and hominoids into Eurasia. In the late Miocene the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] almost completely evaporated before the [[Strait of Gibraltar]] opened. Apes evolved and spread across the Old World, and [[Kelp|kelp]] forests appeared in the seas.

Soviet and later Russian [[Space station|space station]] in [[Low Earth orbit|low Earth orbit]], 1986–2001. Mir was the first modular space station, assembled in orbit from 1986 to 1996, and was the largest artificial satellite until the [[International Space Station]] surpassed it. It was the first continuously inhabited long-term research station in orbit, holding the record for the longest continuous human presence in space until 2010. Valeri Polyakov spent 437 days aboard from 1994 to 1995, the longest single human spaceflight. Visitors from 12 nations conducted experiments in biology, physics, astronomy and meteorology. Mir was the next stage of the [[Soviet space program]]'s station development. It was deorbited in March 2001 after funding was cut off.

Indian poet, one of the principal figures of the Delhi School of the [[Ghazal|ghazal]]. Mir was born in [[Agra]], then called Akbarabad and ruled by the [[Mughal Empire]]. After his father's death he left for [[Delhi]] to finish his education and find patrons. Repeated sacks of Delhi beginning in 1748 led him to move to [[Lucknow]] in 1782, at the invitation of Asaf-ud-Daulah, where he spent the rest of his life. He was one of the pioneers who shaped the [[Urdu]] language, and his poetry is noted for its grief over the decline of Delhi. His autobiography, *Zikr-e-Mir*, is the main source on his life, though it is said to conceal more than it reveals.

American actress. Born in [[Manhattan]], she graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1989. She won an Academy Award and a Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress for playing a sex worker in Woody Allen's comedy *Mighty Aphrodite* (1995). She was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for playing [[Marilyn Monroe]] in *Norma Jean & Marilyn* (1996). Since 2009 she has advocated against [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]].

Hindu mystic poet and devotee of [[Krishna]], venerated as Sant Meerabai in the North Indian Hindu tradition. Born into a Rathore Rajput royal family in Kudki, [[Rajasthan]], she was married in 1516 to Bhoj Raj, crown prince of Mewar, who died of battle wounds in 1521. Her passionate devotion, expressed through music, defied the social and family conventions of her in-laws, who opposed it. Legends say they tried to kill her with poison and a snake, but she was saved by divine intervention. Millions of devotional hymns are attributed to her, but scholars believe only a few hundred are authentic, and most of the earliest written records date from the 18th century. Her hymns, called bhajans, remain famous across [[India]].

Event not explicable by natural or scientific laws, usually attributed to a [[Supernatural|supernatural]] cause. Religions often ascribe miracles to a deity, a miracle worker, a [[Saint|saint]] or a religious leader. Informally, the word also describes any beneficial but statistically unlikely event, such as surviving a [[Natural disaster|natural disaster]]. [[Thomas Jefferson]] held that a true miracle is physically impossible, while [[David Hume]] argued that miracles cannot be confirmed, because every natural explanation can never be ruled out. [[Baruch Spinoza]] described miracles as lawlike events whose causes are unknown. Theologians typically say that [[God]] regularly works through nature but may also act without, above or against it. Naturalistic explanations include errors by witnesses and hallucinations, and British mathematician J. E. Littlewood argued that one-in-a-million events happen to individuals about once a month.

Naturally occurring optical phenomenon in which light bent by [[Refraction|refraction]] forms a displaced image of distant objects or the [[Sky|sky]]. The word comes via French from the [[Latin]] *mirari*, "to look at, to wonder at." Unlike a hallucination, a mirage is a real phenomenon that can be photographed, because light actually forms the false image at the observer's location. In an inferior mirage, which occurs when warm, less dense air lies beneath cooler air, the image appears below the object and is often mistaken for a pool of water. A superior mirage forms when colder air is trapped below warmer air, and a [[Fata Morgana (mirage)|Fata Morgana]] is an elaborate, vertically stacked superior mirage that changes rapidly. [[Convection|Convection]] causes air temperature to vary, creating a [[Refractive index|refractive index]] gradient that blurs the image; heat haze is an inferior mirage seen through heated air. Scientists explained mirages in the 19th century using [[Snell's law]].

Australian model. Born in [[Sydney]] and raised in Gunnedah, she won a 1997 *Dolly* magazine model competition at age 13. She rose to prominence in 2007 as a Victoria's Secret model, the first Australian to be one. Since 2008 she has consistently ranked on the [[Forbes]] list of highest-earning models. She launched the organic skincare brand KORA Organics and has written a self-help book. She was married to actor Orlando Bloom and, since 2017, has been married to [[Snapchat]] CEO [[Evan Spiegel]], with whom she has three children.

South African singer, songwriter and activist against [[Apartheid|apartheid]]. Born in [[Johannesburg]], she began singing professionally in the 1950s. Her brief role in the anti-apartheid film *Come Back, Africa* (1959) brought international attention, and she recorded her first solo album in New York City in 1960. The South African government prevented her return that year, even for her mother's funeral. With [[Harry Belafonte]] she won a Grammy Award for Best Folk Recording for the 1965 album *An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba*. She testified against South Africa at the [[United Nations]] and became involved in the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]]. After marrying [[Black Panther Party|Black Panther Party]] leader Stokely Carmichael in 1968, she lost support among white Americans; her U.S. visa was revoked, and the couple moved to Guinea. She returned to South Africa after apartheid was dismantled in 1990 and died of a heart attack during a concert in Italy.

1975 Soviet avant-garde drama film directed by [[Andrei Tarkovsky]]. Written by Tarkovsky and Aleksandr Misharin, it depicts a dying poet's memories, drawing on Soviet newsreel footage and the poetry of the director's father, Arseny Tarkovsky. Its loosely autobiographical story is nonlinear and moves across prewar, [[World War II|wartime]] and postwar periods, shifting between color, black-and-white and sepia. Critics and audiences were initially polarized, and many found its narrative incomprehensible. The Soviet government approved funding only in 1973 and limited its release amid accusations of "cinephilic elitism." It was later reappraised as Tarkovsky's magnum opus and one of the greatest films of all time.

Object that reflects an image, typically glass coated with a thin layer of metal. Light bounces off a mirror to form an image that is focused by the eye or a lens. Mirrors have been made from stone, metals and glass for thousands of years, including polished [[Obsidian|obsidian]] and metal mirrors in the [[Bronze Age]]. Modern mirrors use [[Silver|silver]] or aluminum for their reflectivity. The silver-backed mirror was invented in 1835 by German chemist [[Justus von Liebig]], who used a chemical reduction process. A mirror reflects light through [[Reflection (physics)|specular reflection]], so a flat mirror yields an undistorted image while a curved mirror may magnify or reduce it. Mirrors are used in [[Telescope|telescopes]], periscopes and rear-view mirrors. According to [[Superstition|superstitions]], breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck.

American [[Punk rock|punk]] band, a pioneer of horror punk. Formed in 1977 in Lodi, New Jersey, by vocalist Glenn Danzig, the band was named after [[Marilyn Monroe]]'s final film, *The Misfits* (1961), and it fused punk with horror-film themes. Its albums *Walk Among Us* (1982) and *Earth A.D./Wolfs Blood* (1983) are considered touchstones of early 1980s hardcore punk. The band disbanded in 1983 but later reformed; bassist Jerry Only, its only constant member, has led it through many lineup changes. [[Metallica]] covered three of its songs on *Garage Inc.*

Hatred of, contempt for, or prejudice against women or girls. A form of [[Sexism|sexism]] that can keep women in a lower social status than men. It includes violence against women, from [[Domestic violence|domestic violence]] to femicide, as well as sexual harassment and legal or social exclusion from full citizenship. Philosopher Kate Manne describes misogyny as the "enforcement arm" of patriarchy, which punishes women who challenge male dominance. The English word, coined in the mid-17th century from Greek *misos* ("hatred") and *gunē* ("woman"), was popularized by second-wave [[Feminism|feminism]] in the 1970s.

Annual international beauty pageant, one of the Big Four. The title was first used by the International Pageant of Pulchritude in 1926, but that contest ended in 1935 amid the [[Great Depression]] and events preceding [[World War II]]. The current pageant was founded in 1952 by Pacific Knitting Mills, a California clothing company, and its first contest was held in [[Long Beach, California|Long Beach]]. [[Donald Trump]] bought the pageant in 1996. It was broadcast on [[NBC]] in the U.S. from 2003 to 2014, and in 2015 NBC cut ties with Trump and the organization over controversial statements about immigrants.

Airborne ranged weapon capable of self-propelled flight, usually aided by a propellant, [[Jet engine|jet engine]] or [[Rocket engine|rocket engine]]. Missiles are classified by launch source and target as surface-to-surface, air-to-surface, surface-to-air or air-to-air, and they typically have targeting, guidance, flight, engine and warhead systems. Rockets preceded missiles, and in the 18th century iron-cased rockets were used in India by the Kingdom of Mysore and [[Maratha Empire]] against the British. The first operational missiles were rocket-based weapons developed by [[Nazi Germany]] in [[World War II]], including the V-1 and [[V-2 rocket|V-2]]. The [[Cold War]] and the development of nuclear weapons then spurred faster, more accurate missiles with longer range. Since the 1980s, attempts to control the spread of long-range missiles, such as the Missile Technology Control Regime (1987), have been voluntary.

[[Sex position]] in which, generally, a woman lies on her back and a man lies on top of her, facing her. The most common sex position, though not universally the most favored, it is often preferred for skin-to-skin contact and eye contact. It is less suitable in late [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. Although one common story credits Christian missionaries, the term likely arose from misunderstandings of [[Alfred Kinsey]]'s 1948 study *Sexual Behavior in the Human Male*.

[[U.S. state]] in the [[Deep South]] region of the United States. It became the 20th state on December 10, 1817, and takes its name from the [[Mississippi River]], which forms its western boundary. By 1860 it was the nation's top [[Cotton|cotton]]-producing state, and enslaved people made up 55% of its population. Mississippi seceded in 1861 and was restored to the Union in 1870. Agriculture and forestry remain major industries, and the state has the lowest per-capita income in the nation. It was a focal point of the [[Civil rights movement]].

Archaeological cultural era in the Southern United States and adjacent Eastern Woodlands, from the end of the 10th century to the 16th century. Mississippian peoples lived in large villages and relied on a diverse agricultural system centered on [[Maize|maize]]. Like their Woodland ancestors, most retained the Hopewell [[Clan|clan]] system, in which each clan functioned like a ritual society. The city of [[Cahokia]], founded in 1050 in [[Illinois]], likely had at least 22,400 people at its peak around 1124. A decades-long drought in Illinois (1150–1200) brought political instability, and Cahokia declined. Mound centers such as Moundville in Alabama and the Yazoo basin in [[Mississippi]] rose in prestige. In the Late Mississippian period (1400–1600), larger paramount chiefdoms emerged, with more defenses and archery.

Landlocked [[U.S. state]] in the Midwestern United States. Missouri entered the United States through the [[Louisiana Purchase]] in 1803, and as the "Gateway to the West" it was central to westward expansion. It was admitted as a slave state under the Missouri Compromise of 1820. As a border state, it was subject to rival governments and guerrilla warfare during the [[American Civil War]]. The largest urban areas are [[St. Louis]] and Kansas City; the capital is Jefferson City. Missouri is the birthplace of ragtime and St. Louis [[Blues|blues]] and is home to Anheuser-Busch, the world's largest beer producer.

Major river in the central United States, the nation's longest. It rises in the Rocky Mountains of southwestern Montana and flows 2,341 mi (3,767 km) before entering the [[Mississippi River]] north of St. Louis, Missouri. It drains more than 500,000 sq mi (1,300,000 km²). Although a tributary, it is slightly longer than the Mississippi and carries a comparable volume of water. For over 12,000 years people relied on it for sustenance and transport, and in the 19th century it was one of the main routes of westward expansion. Fifteen dams impound its main stem, and the river has been channelized for navigation, reducing its length by almost 200 mi (320 km). Development has taken a toll on wildlife, fish populations and water quality.

Ancient Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast [[Anatolia]], with Indo-Aryan linguistic and political influences. Known as Ḫabigalbat in Old Babylonian texts, Ḫanigalbat in Assyrian records and Naharin in Egyptian sources, it existed from about 1550 to 1260 BC. Mitanni was a strong regional power limited by the [[Hittites]] to the north and by Egypt to the west. No royal annals or histories have been found, so knowledge of it depends largely on the texts of its neighbors, including letters to Egyptian [[Pharaoh|pharaohs]] written in [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]]. Its ruling elite showed Indo-Aryan influence and its treaties invoked deities such as Indra, while most of its population was Hurrian.
